facts.summary: Oklahoma's minimum wage is tied to the current federal minimum wage, so it is $7.25 per hour.
facts.notes: Statute text states no employer shall pay 'less than the current federal minimum wage,' so OK tracks the federal rate ($7.25). Verify federal rate has not changed.

facts.summary: Oklahoma has no state daily or weekly overtime law and no higher salary floor; overtime is governed by the federal FLSA (1.5x after 40 hrs/week).
facts.notes: The Oklahoma Minimum Wage Act sets no overtime premium or state salary threshold, so federal FLSA controls. No separate OK overtime statute located.

facts.summary: The Oklahoma Anti-Discrimination Act prohibits employment discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, genetic information, and disability.
facts.notes: Classes largely mirror federal Title VII/ADEA/ADA/GINA. No additional classes (e.g., sexual orientation/gender identity) are enumerated in the statute text reviewed.

facts.summary: Oklahoma's anti-discrimination law defines 'employer' as an entity paying one or more individuals, so it reaches employers of any size with no minimum-headcount threshold.
facts.notes: Broader than federal thresholds (Title VII/ADA 15+, ADEA 20+). Definition covers a legal entity that 'pays one or more individuals a salary or wages.' Confirm no separate size carve-outs elsewhere in Title 25.

facts.summary: A discrimination charge must be filed within 180 days of the last alleged discriminatory act with the Oklahoma Attorney General's Office of Civil Rights Enforcement (or the EEOC); a lawsuit must be filed within 90 days of receiving a Notice of Right to Sue.
facts.notes: Charge filed with the AG's Office of Civil Rights Enforcement (Oklahoma's FEPA, successor to the former Human Rights Commission) or EEOC. Suit is barred more than 90 days after the Right-to-Sue notice.

facts.summary: Oklahoma law makes it a misdemeanor for an employer to discharge, penalize, or otherwise discriminate against an employee for filing a wage/hour complaint with the employer or the Commissioner of Labor, causing an investigation or proceeding to be instituted, or testifying in such a proceeding.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly from the primary statute text (page verified by download). This provision protects reports/complaints/testimony tied to Title 40 wage-and-hour law (Sections 71-198.2); Oklahoma also separately protects reports of occupational health and safety violations (40 O.S. § 403(B)) and, for public employees only, government-wrongdoing reports under the Oklahoma Whistleblower Act (74 O.S. § 840-2.5) -- neither of those two was independently verified against primary text this session.

facts.summary: Oklahoma law voids most traditional non-compete restraints: a general statute bars any contract restraining someone from exercising a lawful profession, trade, or business. A specific carve-out lets an employer and employee agree that, after employment ends, the former employee will not directly solicit the sale of goods or services from the former employer's established customers -- but any other contract provision restraining post-employment competition (e.g., a broader ban on working for a competitor) is void and unenforceable.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against primary statute text (15 O.S. §§ 217-219A, PDF pages 65-67): a former employee is permitted to engage in the same or similar business as the former employer as long as they do not directly solicit established customers; any conflicting contract provision is void. Section 219B separately permits reasonable employee/contractor non-solicitation agreements.

facts.summary: Upon termination (discharge or resignation), Oklahoma requires the employer to pay final wages in full at the next regular designated payday for the pay period in which the work was performed.
facts.notes: Statute does not distinguish discharge vs. resignation; both are paid at the next regular payday. Failure-to-pay exposes employer to liquidated damages (2% of unpaid wages per day, capped at the total unpaid amount).

facts.summary: Oklahoma's Payment of Wages Act sets no limitations period of its own; the general Oklahoma statute of limitations for a liability created by statute (3 years) governs wage and overtime claims.
facts.citation: 40 O.S. § 165.9 (no limitations period specified); 12 O.S. § 95(A)(2) (general 3-year limitation for a liability created by statute)
facts.notes: 12 O.S. § 95(A)(2) allows 'an action upon a liability created by statute other than a forfeiture or penalty' within 3 years; because the Oklahoma Payment of Wages Act (40 O.S. § 165.1 et seq.) does not set its own limitations period, this general 3-year statutory-liability period is understood to apply to Oklahoma wage claims.
